title: 40 actual development days into my AI-assisted point-and-click adventure. Here's where I am
author: milox88
selftext:
Hey everyone! I've been working on L'Eredità Bellini, a classic 2D point-and-click mystery adventure set in Europe.
This has been a dream project of mine for a long time, but realistically it was always far too ambitious for me to build alone. AI changed that  not by coming up with the game for me, but by making it possible for me to actually execute the ideas I already had.
I've logged roughly 40 actual development days so far, and Act I is now playable from beginning to end. It's currently around an hour of gameplay, although there's still a lot of animation and visual polish left to do.
AI has been involved pretty extensively in the production: coding assistance, visual asset generation and iteration, 3D character production, and helping me build some of the tools I needed.
One of those is SceneLab, my own authoring tool for building the game: scenes, dialogue topics, game states, scripted sequences and conditions, photography, object inspection, audio, transitions, etc. It exports everything into the Godot runtime.
Animation has probably been the biggest rabbit hole. I eventually stopped trying to generate final 2D animation frames directly and built a different pipeline:
2D character reference → 3D model → rigged 3D animation → automated sprite baking → transparent 2D atlases → Godot
So the game itself remains completely 2D, while 3D and AI are part of the production pipeline behind it.
I'm currently rebuilding the main character's animations with this system, so the clip is still very much WIP.
The story, characters, puzzles, game design and overall direction are mine. AI does a substantial amount of the execution work, while I design the systems, specify what I need, test it, reject what doesn't work and iterate until it fits the game.
Anyway, this is where the project is after roughly 40 actual development days. It's the first time I've started showing it outside my little development bubble, so I thought this community would probably appreciate seeing what this kind of workflow can actually produce.

comments.author: novokvest
comments.body: Hi! Thanks a lot for sharing your progress! I love visuals for the backgrounds, very cool and immidiatelly speaks Europe, reminds Broken Sword a lot! Now, to be honest I don't like your animations workflow, I think it is a huge overkill, going full 2D would save you hundreds of hours, modern models are capable enough for it, please check out my only post here on reddit. Also if you are interested, I invite you to my discord server dedicated to point and click adventures made with AI, although so far there's only me... And one last thing to note, be prepared for the hatred in regular r/adventuregames/ - they are strict believers of no AI.

replies.author: milox88
replies.body:
Thanks a lot! And the Broken Sword comparison genuinely makes me happy,  that's very close to the atmosphere I'm aiming for.
I read your post, and I completely understand what you mean about my animation workflow being overkill. Honestly, I think your approach is probably the natural end point for this kind of point-and-click production, especially with how quickly video models are improving.
In my case, though, moving to a 2.5D production pipeline was a conscious choice. Having a rigged 3D character that I can reuse for dozens of animations and directions, then bake back into 2D sprites, gives me a level of consistency, control and reusability that's extremely valuable for a project this size.
There's also a very practical limitation on my side: budget and hardware. I'm building this entire game on a low-end laptop from 2019 😄 I simply don't have the GPU to run the kind of local AI workflow you're using.
If I had the budget for a powerful workstation and could run modern models locally at scale, the equation would be very different. Your workflow would become much more attractive, and I'd absolutely experiment with it.
So right now I'm basically trying to find the best compromise between the classic 2D adventure look I love, modern AI-assisted production, and a pipeline that I can actually afford and run reliably as a solo developer.
I really enjoyed reading your post, though. It's fascinating that we're tackling essentially the same problem from different directions . And I'll definitely check out your Discord.
And yes... I've already discovered the r/adventuregames AI rule 😂 Which is unfortunate, because it's probably the most obvious audience for Bellini.

replies.author: novokvest
replies.body: Thanks a lot for taking your time to read my manifesto. I also enjoyed your post and reply! Yeah, in terms of GPU my workflow really pushes close to 24 GB VRAM in various aspects. I haven't mentioned it much, but I believe that when you go for full 2D you gotta train LoRA's(finetunes) for all main characters(those who have more than 2 animations) which is a subject on its own plus requires lots of GPU time. I'd still try image to video generation with MiniMax H3 just to see, it blew my mind back then, I believe [comfy.org](http://comfy.org) provide quite generous free monthly tokens to try it up, maybe hugging face spaces can generate those animations for free, for point and clicks you really need not that many frames. On the other hand I respect when someone stick to their workflows and not switching to new models each month when their weights drop(as I do...) it is better to know a tool well, than to poorly use powerful tool!

replies.author: milox88
replies.body:
Well... I took your advice and actually tried MiniMax H3 😂
I used one of my character pose sheets and generated a simple walking animation. Damn. I wasn't expecting it to work that well.
I'm still very attached to my current 3D → 2D pipeline because of the consistency and control it gives me, so I'm not throwing it away. But I'm now seriously considering experimenting with Comfy + MiniMax in parallel, especially for animations that are difficult to produce with my current workflow.
So thanks, you may have successfully sent me down another rabbit hole 😂

Also, I recently realized that I could just rent a powerful GPU through Google Colab for relatively little money when I actually need it, instead of spending €2.5k on a new PC just to get enough VRAM for this stuff. That makes experimenting with LoRAs and heavier workflows much more realistic for me.

replies.author: novokvest
replies.body: Yup, that's what I'm talking about! You know, yesterday I've actually been thinking about your workflow and there is a major advantage to it - it "feels" retro. Hear me out, doing frame by frame animation was always hard, so back then many adventure games actually utilised drawn or static prerendered backgrounds with 3D characters - Alcatraz, Runaways, Syberia. So your exact clip looks legit, "old school". Modern AI animations instantly recognised as such. If we ever expect to make a dime of those games we would have to deliberately make them less polished.

replies.author: milox88
replies.body:
Funny thing is, that's actually very close to how I ended up with this workflow 😂
My original idea was basically: “I want Broken Sword animations.” So I built a Motion Atlas that extracted the animations from BS1, and my plan was to use those as motion references, generate the corresponding frames with AI, compare them in my tool and manually approve the good ones.
It worked in principle, but I quickly realized I was creating an insane amount of manual work for myself.
Then I had a bit of a revelation looking at games like Runaway and Syberia. I started researching how Pendulo approached their characters and eventually landed on the 3D → 2D/2.5D workflow I'm using now: create the character in 2D, turn it into a consistent 3D model, rig and animate it, then bake the animation back into 2D sprites.
And honestly, I'm pretty happy with it. I can control the animation framerate myself, the results don't look bad at all, and what you said made me realize that some of its limitations may actually be helping the aesthetic rather than hurting it.
I'm using bleeding-edge AI tools to build it, but the feeling I'm deliberately trying to recreate is absolutely that late-90s/early-2000s adventure game look. So maybe chasing perfectly smooth modern AI animation would actually be moving in the wrong direction.

comments.author: Ai_Test_4704
comments.body: I see you have the same issues that drove me mad when I tried to make my game... the images the ai is generating are stunning.. but then, when you charachter moves, he goes through the chair, and outside he is fully disproportional with his sourrounding. The AI sucks at generating any meaningful animation, at least for me.

replies.author: milox88
replies.body:
Yeah, that's exactly the same problem I've been struggling with. The backgrounds and static characters can look great, but animation and keeping everything consistent once things start moving is a completely different story.
I'm actually seriously considering giving ComfyUI + MiniMax a shot for this. I've seen what Novokvest has been experimenting with, and I tried a quick image-to-video test myself. Honestly, the result was much better than I expected.
I'm not sure yet if I'll use it as the final pipeline, but at this point I think it's definitely worth exploring.

comments.author: LocoMod
comments.body: The size of the characters are not proportional to the background.

replies.author: milox88
replies.body: Yep, you're right. Character scaling/perspective is one of the things still on my polish list. Thanks for pointing it out!
